name: Grace Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Grace, thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything here is confidential and won't carry your name, so you can tell me both what you'd say publicly and what you actually think. Is that okay?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, love it. I've been wanting someone to ask me about this for ages, honestly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start with a normal working day. What does it look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior carpenter at a small worker-owned co-op, so the members own the business together and vote on things. We're building twelve timber-frame houses on the old railway yard at the edge of town. I'm usually there by seven, nailing up wall panels, fitting insulation, cutting noggins, which are the short bits of timber between the studs. I'm still bad at reading drawings, so every morning I take a photo of the sheet and ask an AI app to explain what I'm looking at, which my co-workers think is hilarious. What wears me out is the noise of the nail guns all day, and what I love is that by Friday there's a house where there wasn't one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Honestly, that would be a bit of a let-down for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably post something like, well, that was a lot of fuss for a better spellchecker. At work I'd admit I was wrong, because I'm the one who's always saying it'll change everything. Ines would make me buy the coffees for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means not much changes for me, because my job wasn't in the firing line anyway. Thinking AI is a helper for me, not a threat. I'd keep using it to learn faster and I'd be a decent carpenter a few years sooner than I'd otherwise be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am. I'd keep using the apps to understand drawings and check my cut lists before I waste good timber. My gran left me some money two years ago, so I've got well over a year of living saved, and I'd keep that for buying my full member share in the co-op next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit flat, like a film that didn't have an ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it helps you learn faster. Can you give me an example from this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week I had to set out a staircase opening and I was sure I'd mess up the trimmer, which is the heavier joist round the hole. I typed in the measurements and asked it to talk me through it step by step, then I checked with Ines before cutting. Got it right first time, which has never happened to me with stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone at the co-op see that differently from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh yes. Bram, who's been there twenty years, thinks I'm cheating myself. He says you learn by getting it wrong with your own hands. He's probably half right, but I've got it wrong with my own hands plenty, believe me.

S0.say: I'd post that it was a lot of fuss for a better spellchecker. At work I'd admit I was wrong, since I'm the one who always says it'll change everything.
S0.think: Not much changes for me, because my job wasn't in the firing line anyway. AI stays a helper and I'd be a decent carpenter a few years sooner.
S0.do: Keeps working as she does, using AI apps to understand drawings and check cut lists before cutting. Holds her savings, inherited from her gran, for buying her full member share in the co-op next year.
S0.feel: Calm but slightly flat, like a film that didn't have an ending.
S0.quote: Got it right first time, which has never happened to me with stairs.
S0.fieldNote: Grace is openly enthusiastic about AI and uses it daily as a learning crutch for her weak drawing-reading. The plateau disappoints rather than relieves her. Her savings come from an inheritance, and she has a clear goal of buying into the co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: On to the second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's interesting. That's the one where it matters who owns the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, if workers get a share of it. I'd be the annoying person in the co-op meeting with a slideshow about robotic framing tables. Online I'd be arguing that every firm should have to share the savings with the people on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's probably good for me. I'm young, I'm not scared of new kit, and I'm in a business where we vote on what we buy. The ones who'd struggle are the people at the big firms who don't get a say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the co-op to buy a computer-controlled saw that cuts the wall panels from the drawings, which we've talked about. I'd volunteer to be the person who learns to run it, even if that means an evening course. And I'd keep my savings ready for my member share, because I'd want a vote on how the machine gets used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. Like the first day on a new site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the co-op bought that saw, what happens to the people who cut panels by hand now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's me, mostly, and Ines some of the time. In a co-op you can't just sack someone to pay for a machine, it has to go to a vote. I'd want us to agree up front that nobody loses hours, we just build more houses a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the vote went against buying it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be annoyed, but I'd live with it. That's the deal with a co-op, you don't always win. I'd probably bring it back in six months with better numbers.

S1.say: I'd say this is a chance, as long as workers get a share of it. I'd argue online that firms should share the savings with the people on the tools.
S1.think: It's probably good for me: I'm young, not scared of new kit, and in a business where we vote on what we buy. The ones who'd struggle are people at big firms with no say.
S1.do: Pushes the co-op to buy a computer-controlled panel saw and volunteers to learn to run it through an evening course. Keeps her savings ready to buy a member share so she has a vote on how it's used.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited, like the first day on a new site.
S1.quote: In a co-op you can't just sack someone to pay for a machine, it has to go to a vote.
S1.fieldNote: Her progressive views and her comfort with technology fit together through worker ownership. She'd bring in machines herself, but only under a shared deal. She recognises that her calm depends on being in an unusual workplace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oof. Two years. That's not a new saw, that's the whole crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for big public answers, like an income for everyone paid for by taxing the companies that own the AI. I'd be loud about it online and I'd go on marches. And I'd say that co-ops like ours show there's another way to own the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm less worried for me than for most people, and I feel a bit guilty saying that. I've got gran's money, no kids, and I'm good with this stuff. But a co-op of eighteen people can't out-build a company with a thousand robots, so I don't think we'd survive two years either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use my savings to buy my member share straight away, and push the co-op to borrow and buy whatever robots we can, so at least the machines are ours. We'd share out the hours that are left instead of letting people go. And I'd join a campaign for a basic income, which means a regular payment for everyone whether they work or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel like I can still act, but I'd be scared for Ines and Bram and my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about your mum. Why her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She works in a call centre for an energy company. She's fifty-three. She's the one person in my life I think would get hit first and hardest, and she doesn't have savings like I do. I'd probably end up helping her out with gran's money, which is a bit of a circle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put your savings into the co-op's robots. With only two years, is that a safe use of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm being sensible. But I'd rather own a bit of the thing that's replacing me than sit on cash while it loses value. I'd keep some back for mum, maybe a third.

S2.say: I'd say this is the moment for big public answers, like an income for everyone paid for by taxing the companies that own the AI. I'd point to co-ops as another way to own the machines.
S2.think: I'm less worried for myself than for most people, and I feel guilty saying it. But a co-op of eighteen can't out-build a company with a thousand robots, so we probably wouldn't survive two years either.
S2.do: Buys her co-op member share straight away and pushes the co-op to borrow to buy robots it will own. Backs sharing out the remaining hours instead of layoffs and joins a campaign for a basic income, keeping about a third of her savings back for her mum.
S2.feel: Anxious but still able to act, and scared for her co-workers and her mum.
S2.quote: I'd rather own a bit of the thing that's replacing me than sit on cash while it loses value.
S2.fieldNote: She shifts her worry outward to her mum and co-workers, admitting some guilt about her own security. Her instinct is to own the machines collectively rather than fight them. She knows the investment is risky and does it anyway, while holding something back for family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same thing, five years. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's enough to get ready, if you're quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have just enough time to get this right, so let's not waste it on arguing whether it's real. I'd be pushing every union and co-op I know to start planning now. Online I'd be sharing practical stuff, not just doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this one is actually all right for me. Five years is long enough to become the person who runs and fixes the robots on a site, instead of the person they replace. I'm not saying that lasts forever, but it gets me further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a robotics maintenance course in the first year, evenings, and keep working on the frames by day. I'd push the co-op to buy its first robot in year two and make me the one responsible for it. And I'd help set up a group of small building co-ops to share machines, because none of us can afford a fleet alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's more 'let's go' in it than fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'I'm not saying that lasts forever.' What happens after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's real AGI, eventually the robots fix the robots, right? So maybe I get five good years and then I'm in the same boat as everyone else. That's why I keep coming back to who owns them. If I own a slice, the end isn't so scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A plan instead of a scramble. In two years I'm throwing gran's money at it and hoping. In five, I can learn properly, pick the right machine and bring other people along with me.

S3.say: I'd say we have just enough time to get this right, so let's not waste it arguing whether it's real. I'd push unions and co-ops to start planning now and share practical advice online.
S3.think: Five years is enough to become the person who runs and fixes the robots instead of the one they replace. It won't last forever, but it gets me further.
S3.do: Starts an evening robotics maintenance course in the first year while working on frames by day. Pushes the co-op to buy its first robot in year two with her in charge of it, and helps set up a group of small co-ops to share machines.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but with more eagerness than fear.
S3.quote: If I own a slice, the end isn't so scary.
S3.fieldNote: She's clear-eyed that the robot-maintenance role may only buy a few years under real AGI. The extra time turns her from gambling her savings into planning carefully. Shared ownership keeps coming back as her answer to everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one, ten years. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a lot. I'd be thirty-seven, probably still on the tools in some way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for a real transition, and anyone who wastes it should be voted out. I'd be talking about it at the co-op, at the pub, everywhere. I'd also say young builders should be learning this stuff now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I feel pretty good about this one. I'd have time to become a properly good carpenter and also understand the machines. I think there's a decade of work in helping small firms bring this in without wrecking people's lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics course over the next couple of years, without rushing. I'd start teaching other tradespeople to use the AI tools on weekends, maybe charging a bit for it, because people keep asking me anyway. And I'd use AI more and more in my day job, for planning, ordering, checking drawings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like I can see the road ahead, even if it bends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people keep asking you. Who, and what do they ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bram, funnily enough, last month. He wanted to know how I get the app to read a drawing. Also a couple of plumbers I know from another site, and my cousin who does kitchens. It's always the same thing, how do I get it to do the boring part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this picture that bothers you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. That the big firms will use the ten years better than everyone else, buy the best machines early and squeeze the small ones out. Ten years is a long time for money to pile up in a few places.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for a real transition and anyone who wastes it should be voted out. Young builders should be learning this now, not later.
S4.think: I feel pretty good about this one: time to become a properly good carpenter and also understand the machines. There's a decade of work in helping small firms bring it in without wrecking lives.
S4.do: Takes the robotics course over a couple of years without rushing. Starts teaching other tradespeople to use AI tools on weekends for a small fee, and uses AI more in her day job for planning, ordering and checking drawings.
S4.feel: Calm, able to see the road ahead even if it bends.
S4.quote: It's always the same thing, how do I get it to do the boring part.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she sounds settled and even sees a small business teaching others. Her one worry is about power and money concentrating in big firms, which is true to her politics. Bram, the sceptic, coming to her for help is a nice turn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, not really for me but for my mum, Ines, everyone who doesn't have a cushion. What would help is a basic income paid for by taxing the companies that own the AI, and cheap loans so small co-ops like ours can own robots too, not just the big firms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'm sure I'm right. I'm not. I'm excited about this stuff, but I've been excited about things that turned out badly before. Ask me again in five years.

headlineQuote: I'm excited about this stuff, but I've been excited about things that turned out badly before. Ask me again in five years.
portrait: Grace Fischer is a 27-year-old junior carpenter at a worker-owned building co-op, who uses AI every day to make up for weak drawing-reading and has a cushion from her late gran's money. She's progressive, curious and comfortable with risk, and her answer to every picture is that workers should own the machines. She stays calm through the milder pictures and even welcomes change, while the fast AGI picture makes her anxious mainly for her mum and co-workers. With five or ten years she plans to learn robot maintenance, help small co-ops share machines and teach other tradespeople, though she admits she might be wrong.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, less for herself than for her mum and co-workers who don't have a cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income paid for by taxing the companies that own the AI, and cheap loans so small co-ops can own robots too.
